1:
Hezekiah comes to the throne of a kingdom in ruins, and the witnesses open the chapter by measuring both the wreck he inherited and the reform he began at once. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch frame the whole reign as a double undertaking: the pious son of the godless Ahaz recognised that it was the business of his reign to bring the kingdom out of the utterly ruinous condition into which his father's idolatry and heathen policy had sunk it, and to raise the state again in religion, in morals, and in political affairs. He set himself first to do away with idolatry and to restore the worship of the LORD according to the law, and only then to throw off the yoke of Assyria; and Keil observes that the two histories divide the labour differently, the book of Kings dwelling on the Assyrian deliverance while the Chronicle lingers over the cleansing of the temple. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lays out the chapter's course in advance — the opening and repair of the temple doors, the assembling and exhortation of the priests and Levites, the proposal to renew the covenant, the sanctifying and cleansing, the abundant sin-offerings and burnt-offerings, and the rejoicing of king and people.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to the king's very name, reading Yehizqiyahu as though it meant "Strong is Iah," where the book of Kings writes the shorter Hizkiyah, "My strength is Iah," and the annals of Sennacherib preserve the form Hazakiyahu; the mother Abijah, he notes, appears in Kings under the clipped form Abi, and the whole verse corresponds closely to 2 Kings 18:2. The reformed John Gill, treating the two opening verses together, simply anchors the accession and passes the reader to the parallel record.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the bare notice into a lesson on where reform must begin. When Hezekiah came to the crown he applied himself at once to the work; and those who begin with God, Henry says, begin at the right end of their work, and it will prosper accordingly. Those that turn their backs upon God's ordinances may truly be said to forsake God himself — for the neglect of the temple under Ahaz, the unlit lamps that signified the word left unopened and the unburnt incense that signified prayer and praise unoffered, was the very cause of the calamities the nation had lain under. The LORD alone, Henry insists, can prepare the heart of man for vital godliness; and when much good is done in a little time, the glory must be ascribed to him. The witnesses do not divide: together they set Hezekiah at the threshold of his reign, the son of an apostate father turning first, and fast, to the house of God.
2:
The chronicler's verdict on Hezekiah is borrowed word for word from the older history, and the witnesses mark both the borrowing and the standard it invokes — "he did that which was right in the sight of the LORD, according to all that David his father had done." The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott notes simply that the verse is identical with 2 Kings 18:3, and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke likewise sends the reader to his note on that parallel; the chronicler is content to take over the settled judgment of the earlier record unchanged.

Yet the wording the witnesses leave standing carries its own weight. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set this verse at the head of the account of the temple's purification, reading the general commendation as the root of which all that follows is the fruit: because Hezekiah did what was right, he opened the doors, gathered the Levites, cleansed the sanctuary, and renewed the worship. The measure of that rightness is David — not merely a good king but the covenant king, the pattern to which the house of Judah is always held; and "according to all that David his father had done" is a commendation the historian grants to very few, setting Hezekiah apart from the long line of middling and evil kings before him.

The phrase repays a moment's thought, for the father whose steps Hezekiah follows is not the father who begot him. Ahaz had closed the temple and courted the gods of Damascus; his son, reaching back over that near and evil example to the distant and honoured one, takes David for his father instead. The reformation of the whole chapter is contained in that choice of pattern — a king who might have inherited his father's idolatry chooses instead to inherit David's fidelity, and so reverses in a single reign the ruin of the last. The verdict is a title set over all that follows, and the chapter is its proof: the doors flung open, the Levites summoned, the altar served, and the song restored are so many demonstrations that the man did indeed do what was right in the sight of the LORD. The witnesses do not divide. Ellicott and Clarke fix the verse as the chronicler's faithful transcript of the older verdict; Keil makes it the spring of the reform to come. Between them they show that the concrete labours of temple and altar which fill the chapter are no mere ceremonial fussiness but the outworking of one plain thing said of the king at the outset: that he did what was right, and did it by the measure of David.
3:
In the very first month of his very first year, Hezekiah opened the doors of the house of the LORD and repaired them — and the witnesses read in that promptness the whole temper of the reform. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the date against a natural misreading: "the first month" is Nisan, the first month of the sacred year, not the first month of the king's reign, a reckoning he supports from the dating of the cleansing at v.17 and of the later Passover at 2 Chronicles 30:23. The doors Hezekiah opened were the doors his own father had closed, shutting up the temple in the apostasy recorded at 2 Chronicles 28:24; and "repaired them," Ellicott explains, means he overlaid them afresh with metal — bronze or gold-leaf — restoring the plating that had been stripped, as the parallel notice at 2 Kings 18:16 implies.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch weigh the same date and the same act. Hezekiah caused the doors of the house of Jahve to be opened and repaired, the verb for "repaired" being the word used of the temple restoration under Joash at 2 Chronicles 24:12, where it alternates with the word for renewing; and Keil notes the difficulty the commentators find in the date, since the Levites did not finish the cleansing until the sixteenth day of the month, yet the king's summons to them at v.4 must have gone out before the opening. The reformed John Gill adds only that it was the first day of that first month, so that not a day was lost.

The witnesses do not divide, and the bare notice repays their attention. That the first official act of the new reign was to fling open a shut temple is itself the reform in miniature: where Ahaz had barred the doors and quenched the lamps, his son unbars them before he has well settled on the throne. The order of Hezekiah's priorities — the house of God before the business of the kingdom — is the order the witnesses will praise at the next verse; and the repairing of the plundered doors, the mending of what impiety had defaced, is the first stroke of a restoration that will run, door by door and vessel by vessel, through the whole chapter. The gold-leaf laid again upon the temple gates is the visible sign that the worship Ahaz had abandoned is about to be taken up once more.
4:
With the doors open, Hezekiah's first summons goes not to soldiers or counsellors but to the ministers of the sanctuary, and the witnesses attend to where he gathered them and why. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain that the king brought the priests and Levites together "into the open space of the east," the eastern square before the temple, and not, as some had supposed, into the inner court; there he called upon them first to sanctify themselves and then to sanctify the house of the LORD, for they could not proceed to purify the sanctuary except in a state of Levitical purity. The work before them was to carry out all that was unclean, the very abominations of idolatry that Ahaz had brought in; and the king grounded his summons, Keil notes, in the devastation his father had wrought upon the house of God and in the wrath of God that had followed it. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the place of meeting as the eastern square, probably an open area in front of the eastern gate of the sacred enclosure, comparing the like assemblies at Ezra 10:9 and Nehemiah 8:1.

The reformed John Gill marks simply that these were the persons who officiated in the temple service, now called in to be set to their proper work again. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the moral the scene invites: Hezekiah found Judah low and naked after the ruin of Ahaz, yet he did not make it his first business to revive the civil interests of his kingdom but to restore religion to a good posture; and those that begin with God, Wesley says, begin at the right end of their work, and it will prosper accordingly.

The witnesses do not divide. Keil and Ellicott fix the ground on which the assembly stood and the double sanctifying the king required; Gill names the men; Wesley reads the priorities of a wise reformer. Between them they show a king who understood that the cleansing of a nation begins with the cleansing of its worship, and the cleansing of worship with the cleansing of those who lead it. Before a single vessel is scoured or a single sacrifice offered, the ministers themselves must be made clean — for a defiled priesthood cannot purge a defiled temple, and a people cannot be restored to God by hands that are not first themselves surrendered to him. The reform that will fill the chapter is set, at its very outset, upon this order: sanctify yourselves, and then the house.
5:
The king's charge to the Levites opens with a double command — sanctify yourselves, and sanctify the house — and the witnesses gather around both the persons and the pollution to be removed. The reformed John Gill glosses the first clause plainly: the Levites were to sanctify themselves by washing their bodies and their garments, that no defilement might cling to them in their service. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott traces the language through the law and the prophets: "hear me" echoes the summons of earlier reformers at 2 Chronicles 15:2 and 2 Chronicles 20:15; and the "filthiness" to be carried out, the word niddah, denotes properly a personal impurity, as at Leviticus 12:2 and Ezekiel 18:6, and then anything loathsome, as at Ezekiel 7:19 — here the idols and the paraphernalia of their worship.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the charge together with the reasons Hezekiah gives for it in the verses that follow: the fathers have trespassed, forsaken the LORD, turned their backs upon his habitation, shut the doors of the porch, put out the lamps, and left the incense unburnt and the burnt-offerings unoffered in the holy place. That last does not mean, Keil is careful to say, that the legal worship had wholly ceased, but that no burnt-offerings were being brought to the God of Israel — for sacrifices were still being offered, only upon the heathen-patterned altar Ahaz had built. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley names that very abomination: the "filthiness" is the filthy altar Ahaz had set in the place of God's altar, as at 2 Kings 16:11, together with the idols and other detestable things that stood there.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill fixes the ritual washing; Ellicott traces the word for filth through law and prophet; Keil sets the charge against the whole indictment of Ahaz's sacrilege; Wesley points to the counterfeit altar at the heart of the defilement. Between them they show what the reform was up against — not a temple merely dusty from neglect but a sanctuary positively profaned, its true altar displaced by a heathen imitation, its lamps dark and its incense cold. And they show, too, the order Hezekiah keeps: the men before the house, the washing of the body before the carrying-out of the idols. The command to sanctify runs in both directions at once, inward to the ministers and outward to the sanctuary, so that a clean priesthood may bear the unclean things away and the house of God be fit once more for the God whose name it bears.
6:
Hezekiah's charge grounds itself in a frank confession of the fathers' sin, and the witnesses weigh both the crime and the studied gestures by which the verse describes it. The reformed John Gill takes "our fathers have transgressed" of the more immediate ancestors, the king's own father and theirs, whose idolatry was a great trespass — than which, he says, there is no greater evil in the sight of God, nor anything more provoking to him. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens each phrase. "Trespassed" is properly "dealt unfaithfully"; "turned away their faces from the habitation of the LORD" he sets beside the reproach of Jeremiah 2:27, "they have turned their backs unto me, and not their faces," and the sun-worshippers of Ezekiel 8:16; and "turned their backs" is literally "gave neck," an expression whose ordinary sense is "to put to flight," as at Psalms 18:41. It is clear, Ellicott adds, from the next verse that the whole description is meant to fall upon Ahaz and his generation.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the bodily image as the sign of a settled contempt: to turn the back is to have wilfully and obstinately forsaken God and his worship, the very posture a declaration of scorn. What the verse pictures, then, is not a lapse of carelessness but an act of the will — men who did not drift from the sanctuary but deliberately faced away from it.

The witnesses do not divide, and their several notes compose a single portrait of apostasy. Gill weighs the guilt; Ellicott fixes the vivid Hebrew of face and neck and back; Wesley reads the contempt behind the gesture. Between them they let the confession do its proper work. Hezekiah does not soften the charge or spread it thin; he names the sin of the immediate past as unfaithfulness, desertion, and open scorn of the God whose house stood in their midst. And there is a quiet dignity in his including himself — "our fathers," not "your fathers" — owning the guilt of the generation from which he sprang even as he sets himself to undo its work. There is instruction, too, in the vividness Ellicott recovers: the same gesture that in ordinary speech meant to flee before an enemy is here the posture of a nation fleeing from its own God, presenting to him not the face of a worshipper but the back of a deserter. The reform begins, as all true reform must, with an honest reckoning of what went wrong; and what went wrong, the witnesses agree, was that a people turned their faces from the living God, and turned their backs, and walked away.
7:
The indictment grows concrete: the fathers shut the doors of the porch, put out the lamps, and left the incense unburnt and the burnt-offerings unoffered. The witnesses read each item as a specific act of sacrilege. The reformed John Gill notes that to shut up the doors of the porch was to bar all entrance to the temple, so that the house of God stood closed against his people. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott identifies each defaced ordinance in turn: the porch is the entrance to the holy place, the only way into the two holy chambers; the extinguished lamps are those of the great golden stand within; the incense is that of the golden altar. And where the verse says the fathers "have not offered burnt offering in the holy place," Ellicott presses that "the sanctuary" here means not the inner chamber only but the whole sacred precincts, courts and buildings together — the burnt-offerings that Ahaz had presented on his new Syrian altar, described at 2 Kings 16:15, being here counted as nothing at all, because they were irregular and unlawful.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley catches a delicacy in the king's language. Hezekiah says "they," not "my father," Wesley observes, both because it became him as a son to be as tender as he might of his father's name, and because his father would not have done all this had the fathers of the earlier generation not first neglected their duty. The son will confess the sin without parading the shame of the man who begot him.

The witnesses do not divide, and the catalogue of shut doors and quenched lamps repays their care. What Ahaz had done was not merely to add a false worship but to abolish the true — every appointed means of approach to God deliberately stopped: the doors closed so none could enter, the lamps put out so the light of the sanctuary failed, the incense and the burnt-offering ceased so that the daily converse of Israel with her God fell silent. Gill marks the barred doors; Ellicott the darkened lamps and the counterfeit altar whose offerings counted for nothing; Wesley the son's tender reticence over his father. Between them they show why Hezekiah's first labour had to be the opening and cleansing of the house: a temple is not neutral ground when its doors are shut and its fires are cold, but a standing accusation against the people who let it fall silent. To relight the lamps and rekindle the incense is to answer, ordinance by ordinance, the exact sacrilege the fathers had committed.
8:
Hezekiah traces the nation's recent miseries straight to its recent sins — "wherefore the wrath of the LORD was upon Judah and Jerusalem" — and the witnesses agree that the judgment and its cause are of one piece. The reformed John Gill points to how that wrath appeared: God suffered the Syrians, the Israelites, the Edomites, and the Philistines to come up and distress Judah, as the history of the previous chapter had shown. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes on the most dreadful of those blows, the defeat by the northern kingdom in which, he recalls from 2 Chronicles 28:6-8, a hundred and twenty thousand of Judah were slain and two hundred thousand carried captive — a slaughter that made "trouble and astonishment" no exaggeration.

The grammatical-historical witnesses fix the language and its pedigree. Keil and Delitzsch note that "delivered them to trouble, to astonishment, and to hissing" is drawn from the covenant curses of Deuteronomy 28:25 and the prophetic threats of Jeremiah 24:9, and that "as ye see with your eyes" points the Levites to the visible ruin Ahaz had brought — the defeats at the hands of Syrians, Ephraimites, Philistines, and Edomites. Charles Ellicott renders the phrase more starkly, "made them a horror, an astonishment, and a hissing," calling the language Deuteronomic and comparing the same triad at Deuteronomy 28:37 and Jeremiah 25:9; the people had only to look about them, he says, to behold the disastrous results of the invasions and of the appeal to Assyria recorded in the preceding chapter.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the pastoral point from the word "hissing": the nation had been reduced to such calamities that all who saw or heard of them were astonished, and hissed at a people who by their own sin and folly had brought such misery upon themselves. And Wesley presses the lesson home for every reader: when we are under the rebukes of God's providence, it is good to enquire whether we have not neglected God's ordinances, and whether that be not the controversy he has with us. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Clarke count the wounds; Keil and Ellicott trace the Deuteronomic language of the curse; Wesley reads the whole as a summons to self-examination. Between them they let Hezekiah's argument stand plain: the sword and the captivity were no accident of politics but the kindled anger of God against a people who had shut his doors, and the only cure for a wrath so incurred is the reconciliation the king is about to seek.
9:
The king presses the proof of God's anger into the very households of his hearers — the fathers fallen by the sword, the sons and daughters and wives carried into captivity — and the witnesses read the verse as the pivot from lament to resolve. The reformed John Gill refers the slaughter to the great numbers who fell before the kings of Syria and Israel, the disaster of the previous reign still fresh in every family. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds a mitigating note from the same history: though the verse speaks of captivity, the captives taken by Israel had in fact been presently released, as the mercy shown at 2 Chronicles 28:14-15 records — so that the wound, grievous as it was, had not been left wholly without relief.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the sentence forward into the purpose it serves. It is to turn away this anger of God that Hezekiah declares his intent to make a covenant with the LORD — that is, to renew the covenant by restoring the worship that had been abandoned; and it is on that ground that he calls upon the Levites not to be slack in the duty entrusted to them. Keil notes the tenderness of the address that follows, the king calling the Levites "my sons" in the affectionate manner of a father instructing his children, and observes that the word he uses for their negligence, occurring only here in this form, means to let a thing fall through carelessness or sloth. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds only that the opening "For" is better rendered "And," and sends the reader back to the invasions of 2 Chronicles 28:5-8 for the calamities the verse recalls.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill numbers the slain; Wesley recalls the captives' release; Keil binds the sorrow to Hezekiah's resolve and marks the fatherly warmth of his charge; Ellicott mends the conjunction. Between them they show the king doing what a true reformer must: he will not let his people take refuge in vague regret, but sets the ruin before them in its sharpest and most domestic form — your fathers dead, your children and wives dragged away — and then, having named the wound, he names the remedy. The recital of the disaster is not despair but the ground of a new beginning; for once a people can be brought to see that their misery grew out of their sin, they can be brought also to see that their recovery must grow out of their return. It is precisely there, in the resolve to make a covenant, that the next verse will turn.
10:
Out of the confession of guilt rises the king's great purpose — "now it is in mine heart to make a covenant with the LORD God of Israel" — and the witnesses read the resolve as the true heart of the reform. The reformed John Gill takes it as the renewing of a covenant, after the manner of Asa and of Jehoiada before him, a solemn engagement to serve the LORD and to worship him according to his own will. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it likewise as the renewal of that national covenant under which the whole people were constantly held, whose sign was circumcision and whose very spirit was the ancient pledge, "I will be your God; ye shall be my people." The covenant Hezekiah proposes is thus no new invention but the recovery of an old bond that Ahaz had broken.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott brings his usual precision to the phrasing. "Now it is in mine heart" is a construction he traces through 1 Chronicles 22:7 and 1 Chronicles 28:2; the preposition in "make a covenant with" is properly "for"; and "that his fierce wrath may turn away" is literally "return," the same verb as at Isaiah 5:25, the very anger of God bidden to turn back from the people as at Numbers 25:4.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill sets the covenant in the succession of Judah's reformers; Clarke recovers its ancient terms; Ellicott fixes the grammar of the resolve and the turning-away of wrath. Between them they show the inward spring of the whole chapter. Hezekiah's aim is not merely to tidy a neglected temple or to restore a lapsed ceremony, but to heal the ruptured relation between the LORD and his people — to bind the nation again, by a deliberate act of the will, to the God it had forsaken, and so to see the kindled anger of v.8 turned away. The phrase "it is in mine heart" marks the reform as a thing conceived in the king's own bosom, not imposed by disaster alone; and the covenant he purposes is the frame into which every act that follows — the cleansing, the sacrifice, the song — will be set. And the witnesses are careful that the covenant is God's before it is the king's: Hezekiah does not invent new terms but returns to the old pledge, so that the renewal is less a fresh bargain than a coming home to a bond that had never lapsed on God's side, however grievously it had been broken on Israel's. All of it is the outward shape of one inward resolve: to be the LORD's people again, and to have the LORD again for their God.
11:
Hezekiah closes his charge with an appeal at once tender and urgent — "my sons, be not now negligent" — and the witnesses dwell on the fatherly warmth of the address and the dignity of the office it presses. The reformed John Gill notes that the king speaks of the Levites as their father would, in the most tender and affectionate manner. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley presses the point further: he calls them sons though many of them were older than himself, because by his tender love and affection, as by his office, he was bound to be a nursing father to them; and the negligence he warns against is a slackness both in sanctifying themselves and the temple, and in quickening and preparing themselves and the people for God's service.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms that "my sons" is a condescending term of endearment from the king, just as "my father" was a term of respect for a prophet, as at 2 Kings 2:12 and 2 Kings 13:14; and he marks the emphatic pronoun in "you hath the LORD chosen to stand before him," the very ground of the summons. Ellicott adds, in his critical way, that the thought and style of the whole royal address make it plainly a free composition after the manner of the ancient historians — the sense of Hezekiah's words rather than a stenographer's record. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the substance of the appeal: the LORD had chosen the Levites to stand before him, to serve him, to minister to him, and to burn incense; and this address, heard with gladness, moved them at once to the work.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Wesley hear the fatherly love in "my sons"; Ellicott secures the endearment and the emphatic election; Keil names the fourfold office to which the Levites were chosen. Between them they show the king appealing not to fear but to honour — reminding the ministers that theirs is no drudgery but a chosen nearness to God, a standing before him that kings might envy. Negligence in such an office is not merely a failure of diligence but a contempt of privilege; and it is by lifting the Levites' eyes to the dignity of their calling, rather than by threat, that Hezekiah rouses them. The next verse will show how well the appeal landed, for at these words the Levites rise.
12:
The king's appeal is answered on the instant — "then the Levites arose" — and the witnesses turn to the roll of names by which the chronicler records the response. The reformed John Gill goes through the whole list, numbering two men from each of the great Levitical houses: two Kohathites, Mahath and Joel; two Merarites, Kish and Azariah; two Gershonites, Joah and Eden; two of the family of Elizaphan; two of the family of Asaph, one of the chief singers in David's day; two of the family of Heman, another of the principal singers; and two of the family of Jeduthun, the third, whom Gill identifies with Ethan — fourteen in all. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the pattern, that the verse enumerates two members of each of the three great Levitical subtribes, Kohath, Merari, and Gershon; he notes that Mahath and Eden recur among Hezekiah's officers at 2 Chronicles 31:13-15, and that Kish son of Abdi and Joah son of Zimmah had appeared in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles 6:21 and 1 Chronicles 6:44, so that these look to be family rather than merely personal names.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the same fourteen in order and explain the design behind them: two Levites from each of the three ancestral families, then two of the house of Elizaphan — that is, Elzaphan son of Uzziel son of Kohath, named at Exodus 6:18, who in the time of Moses was prince of the family of Kohath at Numbers 3:30 — and then two from each of the three musical guilds of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun. The heads of the houses, having heard the king's word with gladness, assembled their brethren and set to work.

The witnesses do not divide, and the catalogue they patiently unfold is more than a clerk's list. That the chronicler names the fourteen, house by house, is his way of showing that the response to Hezekiah's appeal was neither partial nor grudging: from every branch of Levi — the ancient ministering families and the singers alike — men rose up by name to undertake the cleansing. Gill and Ellicott recover the persons and their genealogies; Keil lays bare the deliberate symmetry of two from each house. Between them they let the roll speak the thing it was set down to say: that when the king called, the whole tribe of Levi answered, and answered in the persons of known and willing men who put their own hands to the work of restoring the house of God.
13:
The chronicler completes his roll of the Levitical heads with the names of the singers' houses, and the witnesses attend to the families that now come forward. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch continue the enumeration through this verse — of the sons of Elizaphan, Shimri and Jeiel; of the sons of Asaph, Zechariah and Mattaniah — and read the whole assembly of fourteen as the heads of the various families and branches of Levi, who, having gathered their brethren and all sanctified themselves, went forward with the cleansing of the temple according to the command of the king. That command, Keil is careful to note, rested "by the words of the LORD," being founded upon the ordinances of the Mosaic law, a phrase he compares with the like construction at 2 Chronicles 30:12.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fills in the pedigree of the house named first: the sons of Elizaphan are the descendants of Elzaphan son of Uzziel son of Kohath, named at Exodus 6:18, who was prince of the sons of Kohath in the time of Moses at Numbers 3:30; two of this leading house, and two of the Gershonite Asaphites, are here recorded as present and willing.

The witnesses do not divide, and the appearance of the singers' families at this point is worth marking. Asaph stands at the head of one of the three great guilds of temple music that David had established; that his sons are numbered among those who set their hands to the cleansing shows that the reform drew in not only the ministering priests and the ancient ancestral houses but the choristers too — the very men whose voices will fill the temple with the song of the LORD when the sacrifices begin at v.27. Keil binds the whole company to the double authority under which they acted, the king's command grounded in God's word; Ellicott secures the ancestry of Elizaphan's house. Between them they show a cleansing carried out in order and by warrant: every family of Levi represented, every man sanctified, and all of them moving at a royal command that was itself only the echo of a higher one, the written word of the LORD by which the whole work was measured and made lawful. The restoration is not improvised zeal but obedience — the king commanding, the Levites answering, and the law of Moses governing them both.
14:
With the naming of the houses of Heman and Jeduthun the roll of the Levitical heads is complete, and the witnesses pause over the last of the fourteen. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott records that here two Levites of each of the remaining musical guilds — the Kohathite sons of Heman and the Merarite sons of Jeduthun, whom he identifies with Ethan — are finally named, making up, with the pairs already given, a total of seven pairs, or fourteen principal men of the Levitical order; he refers the reader to the genealogies of the singers at 1 Chronicles 6:18-32, and notes that the Jehiel named here recurs among Hezekiah's overseers at 2 Chronicles 31:13.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set down the same names in their order — of the sons of Heman, Jehiel and Shimei; of the sons of Jeduthun, Shemaiah and Uzziel — completing the fourteen heads who, having sanctified themselves, went forward to purify the house. The reformed John Gill had already gathered the whole company into his tally, reckoning Jeduthun the third of the principal singers and the same man as Ethan, and counting the two houses of Heman and Jeduthun as the last of the seven pairs.

The witnesses do not divide, and the completing of the roll with the three musical guilds is itself instructive. The families of Asaph, Heman, and Jeduthun were the singers David had appointed to the service of song in the house of the LORD; that their heads stand among the fourteen who undertook the cleansing shows how thoroughly the reform reached into every order of the Levites. It was not left to a few ministering priests to purge the temple while the choristers waited idle; the singers themselves put their hands to the carrying-out of the filth, so that the same men who would soon lift up the psalms of David and Asaph first stooped to clear the defilement of Ahaz. Ellicott and Keil recover the last names and the neat total of seven pairs; Gill fixes the identity of Jeduthun with Ethan. Between them they show a cleansing undertaken by the whole strength of Levi, ministers and musicians alike — every house named, every head sanctified, and the temple's own singers among the first to labour for its restoration. The roll of fourteen is the chronicler's quiet testimony that when the king called, no branch of the tribe held back.
15:
The heads of the houses now gather their brethren and set the whole company to the sanctifying, and the witnesses attend to the authority under which they moved. The reformed John Gill notes simply that they gathered their brethren and sanctified themselves, as they had been bidden. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott explains that as chiefs and heads of houses they had the requisite authority to summon their brethren, the families most concerned being those that dwelt in Jerusalem; and he presses the crucial phrase, that they came "according to the commandment of the king, by the words of the LORD" — that is, through the words of Jehovah, the royal mandate itself resting upon the written Law, a construction he compares with 1 Chronicles 25:5 and with the like notice at v.25 below, "for by the hand of Jehovah was the commandment."

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the clause the same way: the fourteen heads assembled the other Levites who dwelt in Jerusalem, all sanctified themselves, and went forward with the cleansing according to the command of the king, which was itself founded upon the words of the LORD, the commands of Moses' law, as at 2 Chronicles 30:12. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley turns to the work itself: to cleanse the temple was to clear it of the dirt it had contracted while it stood so long shut up — the dust, the cobwebs, the rust upon the vessels — and much more of the idols and idolatrous altars that had been set up within it.

The witnesses do not divide, and the double warrant they recover is the point worth holding. The Levites did not act on their own zeal, nor merely at the king's word, but at a royal command that was itself grounded in the command of God. Ellicott and Keil both fasten on the phrase "by the words of the LORD," and rightly, for it marks the whole reform as obedience twice over: human authority moving under divine, the king's mandate valid precisely because it echoed the written law. Gill fixes the gathering and the sanctifying; Wesley pictures the homely labour of clearing dust and rust as well as idols. Between them they show a cleansing that was orderly, authorised, and lawful — not a mob's iconoclasm but the appointed ministers, sanctified and summoned, doing at the king's word what the word of God had all along required. The reform of the temple is thus set squarely upon the law of the temple's own God.
16:
The cleansing now moves inward, and the witnesses mark with care the division of labour that the law imposed upon it. The reformed John Gill explains that the priests went into the inner part of the house, the holy place where the candlesticks and the shewbread tables stood, into which none but priests might enter — and, in the case of necessity, even into the most holy place, though that was reserved to the high priest on the day of atonement, others being admitted only for such needful work as repairs or, as here, cleansing. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the whole chain of the work: the priests went into the interior to cleanse it and brought out all the uncleanness they found into the court, whence the Levites carried it away out of the precincts to the brook Kidron; for the Levites were forbidden by the law to enter the holy place, and this command, Keil observes, was strictly kept. What the defilements were cannot now be exactly known — vessels used in the idol-worship of Ahaz, perhaps, together with the ordinary filth that neglect had gathered upon the sacred furniture.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sets out the sequence in days: the priests and Levites cleansed first the courts, both of the priests and of the people, spending eight days upon that labour; then they cleansed the interior of the temple, but since the Levites might not enter, the priests carried all the dirt and rubbish out to the porch, where the Levites collected it and cast it into the Kidron — and in this a further eight days were spent, so that the whole purification took sixteen days. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the arrangement: the interior of the Temple proper, which the Levites might not enter but only the priests, according to the legal rule; the "uncleanness," a word he distinguishes from the niddah of v.5; and the brook Kidron, better the Wady of Kidron, the same channel down which later reformers cast the idols they destroyed, as at 2 Kings 23:12.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott fix the legal boundary that kept the Levites out of the holy place; Keil and Clarke trace the relay by which priests bore the filth to the court and Levites carried it to the valley. Between them they show a cleansing conducted with scrupulous regard for the very order it was restoring: even in purging the temple of idolatry, the ministers would not transgress the law of the temple, the priests within and the Levites without, each keeping his appointed place. The filth of Ahaz was carried off to the Kidron; but the holiness of the house was honoured in the very manner of its cleansing.
17:
The chronicler dates the whole work with unusual exactness, and the witnesses follow the calendar he keeps. The reformed John Gill notes that they began on the first day of the first month to sanctify — whether of the king's reign or, rather, of the year, the month being Nisan, which the Targum here calls Ab. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch lay out the two stages: on the first day of the first month they commenced with the purification of the courts; on the eighth day they came to the porch of the LORD and with it began the cleansing of the temple building itself, which lasted eight days more, so that the whole was finished on the sixteenth day of the first month. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott gives the same reckoning — the courts cleansed by the eighth of Nisan, when they "came to the porch," the entry of the holy place, and the two holy chambers cleansed in the following eight days, the work done by the sixteenth.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley lifts the bare date into a meditation. "The first day" — a happy beginning of the new year! Thus, he says, should every year begin, with the reformation of what is amiss and the purging away of all the defilements contracted in the year foregoing. The turning of the calendar and the turning of the heart are set side by side.

The witnesses do not divide, and the precision of the record is itself eloquent. Sixteen days, in two even stages, from the outer courts to the inner chambers — the chronicler counts them because the completeness of the cleansing mattered, and because a work begun on the first day of the sacred year and finished before its middle bore the mark of a nation setting its whole reckoning of time under the service of God. Gill weighs the calendar; Keil and Ellicott trace the two eight-day stages from court to holy place; Wesley reads the new year's dawn as a summons to fresh reformation. Between them they show the restoration proceeding not by fits and starts but by an ordered progress inward, from the common courts to the holy chambers, until every part of the house had been reclaimed. The temple that Ahaz had shut up and defiled was, in sixteen measured days, made clean again from the outer gate to the inner sanctuary — and the year that opened upon that cleansing was, as Wesley says, a happy beginning indeed.
18:
The work finished, the Levites go in to the king with their report, and the witnesses attend both to the errand and to the sacred furniture they name as restored. The reformed John Gill notes simply that they went in to Hezekiah in his palace to tell him the temple was cleansed. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch give the substance of the report: they had cleansed all the house of the LORD, the altar of burnt-offering with all its vessels, and the table of shewbread with all its vessels — and Keil identifies the vessels that Ahaz had "thrown away," made worthy of rejection, as the copper altar of burnt-offering, the brazen sea, and the lavers upon their bases, named at 2 Kings 16:14-17. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds his philological notes: they went in "to the interior" of the palace; the altar of burnt-offering was the one Ahaz had superseded and displaced from its legal position, as at 2 Kings 16:14-15; and the shewbread table is literally "the table of the pile" of sacred cakes, only one such table being here mentioned, whose metal work, like all the sacred apparatus, would have been badly tarnished by neglect alone, apart from any wanton misuse.

The witnesses do not divide, and the inventory they recover repays notice. The report is not a vague assurance that all is well but a careful naming of what has been reclaimed — the great altar, the table, and their vessels, the very furniture on which the daily worship of Israel depended and which Ahaz had cast aside for his heathen imitations. That the Levites can render so precise an account is itself a mark of the thoroughness of the work: nothing was left in doubt, nothing overlooked. Gill fixes the errand; Keil names the altar, the sea, and the lavers that had been rejected; Ellicott secures the sense of the displaced altar and the tarnished table. Between them they show the ministers standing before the king to declare, item by item, that the house is clean and its holy things are set in order once more — the outward proof that the covenant Hezekiah purposed in his heart has begun to take concrete shape in bronze and gold and cleansed stone. The next verse will complete the report with the vessels Ahaz had profaned, now prepared and sanctified and standing ready before the altar of the LORD.
19:
The Levites round off their report with the vessels Ahaz had profaned, now recovered and made ready, and the witnesses weigh the exact charge against the former king. The reformed John Gill observes that Ahaz did not literally throw the vessels away, for they were valuable, being of gold and silver; rather, as Kimchi interprets, he removed them and turned them to idolatrous uses, or, as the Targum has it, he defiled and profaned them, making them abominable by the service of strange idols. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott fixes the language: "cast away" is the same word rendered "cast off" at 2 Chronicles 11:14; the vessels so treated were the brazen altar, the brazen sea, and the lavers on their stands, named at 2 Kings 16:14-17; "in his transgression" means in his unfaithfulness or apostasy; and "have we prepared" means we have ordered them aright, put them to rights, so that they now stand before the altar of the LORD.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the clause as the completion of the report and the threshold of the re-dedication: all the vessels Ahaz had cast away in his transgression are prepared and sanctified and set before the altar, ready for the sacrifices that the king will offer at v.20. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gives the Targum's fuller paraphrase, that the vessels Ahaz had polluted and rendered abominable by strange idols the Levites had gathered and hidden, replacing them with others they had prepared, all now standing before the Lord.

The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley draws the comfort the verse holds out: though the vessels of the sanctuary may be profaned for a while, God will find a time and a way to sanctify them again; neither his ordinances nor his obedient people shall be suffered to fail for ever. The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Clarke weigh the several senses of Ahaz's crime — removed, profaned, hidden away; Ellicott fixes the words and names the sacred vessels; Keil sets them ready before the altar; Wesley reads in their recovery a pledge of God's power to reclaim what impiety defiles. Between them they show the cleansing complete not only in the fabric of the house but in the holy things that furnish it: the very vessels a wicked king had turned to idol-service are washed, restored, and set out again for the worship of the true God, a visible token that no sacrilege is final where God intends to restore.
20:
The house being cleansed, the king loses not a moment in coming to worship, and the witnesses mark both his promptness and the sacrifices he brings. The reformed John Gill notes that Hezekiah rose early, taking the first opportunity to attend the service of God and to set an example to his people. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sets the same rising against the psalmist's morning prayer at Psalms 5:3, and explains why the king gathered only the rulers of the city: there was no time to send out a general summons to the country, for he wished to proceed at once with the sacrifices of expiation, and so assembled the chief men of Jerusalem and went up without delay to the house of the LORD.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the theology out of the haste. As soon as Hezekiah heard the temple was ready, he lost no time; atonement must be made for the sins of the last reign, and it was not enough to lament and forsake those sins — they brought a sin-offering. Our repentance and reformation, Henry insists, will not obtain pardon but in and through Christ, who was made sin, that is, a sin-offering, for us. And he notes the temper of the whole solemnity: while the offerings were upon the altar the Levites sang, for sorrow for sin must not prevent us from praising God; the king and the congregation gave their consent to all that was done, since it is not enough to be where God is worshipped if we do not ourselves worship with the heart. We should offer up our spiritual sacrifices of praise and thanksgiving, Henry urges, and devote ourselves and all we have, as sacrifices acceptable to the Father only through the Redeemer.

The witnesses do not divide. Gill and Ellicott fix the king's eager rising and the reason he summoned the city rather than the countryside; Henry reads the sin-offering as the type of Christ and the whole scene as a pattern of heart-worship. Between them they show the re-dedication beginning as it ought — not with self-congratulation over a temple made clean, but with a sacrifice for sin, the king humbling himself and his people before the altar they had restored. The cleansing of the house was the outward work; the atonement now offered upon its altar is the inward reality, the acknowledgment that a purged temple avails nothing without a pardoned people. And Henry's eye, running from the slain victim to the Redeemer it prefigured, reads in Hezekiah's early-morning offering the whole gospel logic of the chapter: that reformation opens the door, but only sacrifice makes the peace.
21:
The sacrifices of expiation are brought in extraordinary number — seven bullocks, seven rams, seven lambs, and seven he-goats — and the witnesses explain both the count and the three objects for which atonement is made. The reformed John Gill reads the offerings as atonement in a typical way, having respect to the sacrifice of the Messiah: for the sins of the king and his family and court, among whom idolatry had prevailed under Ahaz; for the cleansing of the temple, which his idolatries had polluted; and for the expiation of the whole land. Seven of each sort are ordered, Gill notes, though the law required but one goat for a sin-offering, because of the multitude of the transgressions and the length of time in which the sacrifices had been neglected.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses press the same point. Adam Clarke observes that this was far more than the law required, which at Leviticus 4:13 ordered one calf for the sins of the people and one he-goat for the prince; but the law spoke only of sins of ignorance, whereas here were sins of every kind and every dye — idolatry, apostasy, profanation of the temple — the sin-offerings being made first for the kingdom, that is the king and his family; second for the sanctuary, defiled and its priests profaned; and finally for Judah, the whole people led into abomination. John Wesley reads the number the same way: seven is customary in sacred matters, and is used here in regard of the vast numbers and various kinds of sins whose guilt lay upon the kingdom, many and presumptuous, not the single sin of ignorance for which one bullock would suffice.

The grammatical-historical witnesses supply the ritual frame. Keil and Delitzsch note that the burnt-offerings are named first, as in the sacrificial law of Leviticus, though the sin-offering was in fact presented before them, and that the king commanded the priests, the sons of Aaron, to offer them upon the altar. Charles Ellicott calls it an extraordinary sacrifice for an extraordinary occasion, comparing the seven bullocks and seven rams of Numbers 23:1 and the sin-offerings of the returned exiles at Ezra 6:17, and stressing that all was done in careful accordance with the rule of the Torah. The witnesses do not divide. All agree that the sevenfold offering answered a sin sevenfold in its enormity, and that its threefold aim — kingdom, sanctuary, and people — reached to every quarter that Ahaz's apostasy had defiled; and Gill and Wesley alike hear beneath the slain goats the one true sacrifice they prefigured, without which no multitude of victims could take sin away.
22:
The ritual of the blood now begins, and the witnesses, though few here, attend closely to its careful order. The reformed John Gill notes simply that the priests killed the seven bullocks first, as the victims were brought in their appointed sequence. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the whole action: they killed the bullocks, and the priests received the blood and sprinkled it upon the altar; likewise when they had killed the rams they sprinkled the blood, and again with the lambs — each kind slain and its blood dashed against the altar in turn.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott brings his philologist's care to every clause. "Received the blood" means the priests caught it in the bowls of sprinkling; "sprinkled it on the altar" is rather that they threw it against, or literally towards, the altar, the same rite prescribed at Leviticus 8:19. He marks the deliberate symmetry of the verse — the three clauses for bullocks, rams, and lambs cast in parallel — and reads the repetition as a mark of the writer's anxiety to show how carefully the legitimate ritual was observed in each instance. And he fixes the verb "killed" as the word shachat, to slaughter, the term specially used of the slaying of sacrificial victims, as at Leviticus 1:5.

The witnesses do not divide, and the repetition Ellicott notes is the very point of the verse. The chronicler could have said in a word that the animals were killed and their blood offered; instead he sets down each stage three times over, bullock and ram and lamb, kill and receive and sprinkle, precisely to display the exactness of a worship restored to the letter of the law. Gill marks the order; Keil traces the blood from knife to altar; Ellicott recovers the bowls, the throwing of the blood, and the symmetry of the clauses. Between them they show that after the long irregularity of Ahaz's reign — his foreign altar, his counterfeit rites — the first thing Hezekiah's priests are careful to get exactly right is the handling of the blood, on which the whole meaning of atonement hangs. The blood dashed against the altar is the visible pledge that a life has been given for the guilt confessed; and that it is offered thrice, in scrupulous order, is the chronicler's way of saying that lawful worship has come home to Judah, and that the God who was served so carelessly under Ahaz is served now with reverent and measured obedience.
23:
The he-goats of the sin-offering are brought forward last, and upon them the king and the assembly lay their hands — a gesture the witnesses read as the heart of the whole expiation. The reformed John Gill notes that the goats were brought before the king and the congregation because they were to make atonement for the sins of both. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the laying-on of hands as an act of confession: they confessed their sin, and, having by their transgression forfeited their own lives, they offered these animals to die as vicarious offerings, their life taken for the life of their owners. The substitution is plain — the guilty lay their hands upon the innocent, and the innocent dies in their room.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott secures the language and the law. "Brought forth" is rather "brought near," to the altar; the goats are called by the classical Hebrew word for "hairy ones," where the earlier verse at v.21 had used a later, Aramaic term; and the laying-on of hands, he shows from Leviticus 4:4, was the rite by which the offerer pressed his hand upon the victim's head, whether the sacrifice were a burnt-offering, a thank-offering, or a sin-offering, its natural fitness in the case of an expiatory sacrifice being obvious. Here, Ellicott observes, "the king and the congregation" performed it on behalf of the entire nation. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley says the same in brief: it was the king and the elders of the congregation who laid on their hands, in the name of the whole people.

The witnesses do not divide, and the theology they draw from the gesture is one. To lay the hand upon the head of the victim was to transfer, in solemn symbol, the sin of the confessor to the beast that was about to die; and that Hezekiah and the rulers did it for the whole nation makes the sin-offering a public, representative act — the sins of Judah gathered up and laid upon the goats, and the goats slain in Judah's stead. Gill fixes the double atonement for king and people; Clarke and Ellicott and Wesley alike expound the substitution and the representation. Between them they show the innermost meaning of the day's sacrifice, and the innermost pointer to the gospel it prefigured: guilt confessed, guilt transferred, and the guiltless dying that the guilty might live. The hands pressed upon the he-goats are the hands of a whole nation owning its sin and laying it, by faith, upon another — the very posture in which, the witnesses have already hinted, the true Sin-offering would one day be received.
24:
The priests kill the goats and make atonement with their blood, and the witnesses fasten on the sweep of that atonement — for the king had commanded it to be made "for all Israel." The reformed John Gill notes only that the priests killed the seven he-goats, the killing of the bullocks, rams, and lambs having been recorded before. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch carry the rite to its end: the priests killed them and made reconciliation with their blood upon the altar, to make an atonement for all Israel, for the king commanded that the burnt-offering and the sin-offering should be made for all Israel.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott explains the ritual and presses the wide phrase. "Made reconciliation with their blood" is literally "made sin-offering of their blood," the rite whose meaning appears from Leviticus 4:30: the priest dipped his finger in the blood of the victim and touched the horns of the altar, then poured the rest at its base. And "for all Israel," Ellicott insists, is no loose expression — it includes the northern kingdom; for Hezekiah's atonement reached in intention beyond Judah to the ten tribes, a purpose he would carry further in the invitation to their people to keep the Passover at 2 Chronicles 30:1.

The witnesses do not divide, and it is that phrase "for all Israel" that gives the verse its reach. Judah alone had cleansed the temple and brought the offerings; yet the atonement made upon the restored altar was pronounced, by the king's own command, for all Israel — for the scattered and apostate northern tribes as well as for the southern kingdom that had gathered to worship. Gill marks the slaying; Keil fixes the command that widened the atonement; Ellicott recovers the blood on the horns and at the base of the altar, and the deliberate embrace of the north. Between them they show a Hezekiah whose vision overleapt the border of his own realm. The sacrifice offered in Jerusalem was meant to cover a people long divided; and in commanding atonement for "all Israel," the king reached toward a unity that the sword had broken and that only the altar might begin to heal — a reach that the great Passover of the next chapter would make explicit, when messengers went out to Ephraim and Manasseh to call the remnant of the north home to the God of their fathers.
25:
With the sacrifices ordered, Hezekiah restores the temple music, and the witnesses trace the instruments, their Davidic origin, and the prophetic authority behind them. The reformed John Gill notes that the king set the Levites in the house of the LORD with cymbals, psalteries, and harps, the three principal instruments of religious worship, which had fallen into disuse in the days of Ahaz. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms that Hezekiah restored the ancient choral worship as David had established it at 1 Chronicles 23:5, and dwells on the sanction the verse claims: this is the only place where the institution of the Levitical minstrelsy is ascribed to the injunctions of the prophets Gad and Nathan, yet the thing is probable in itself, for no great step, civil or religious, would be taken by a king without consulting the divine will through his prophets, and prophecy was intimately bound up with music. "For so was the commandment of the LORD by his prophets," Ellicott reads, means that David's command was obeyed because it was divine, having come through the prophets who represented Jehovah.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees that David introduced these instruments into the worship of God, but turns the note into a long protest. Moses, he observes, had appointed no musical instruments for the tabernacle; the trumpets then used were not for song but, like bells, to give notice to the congregation; it was David who brought in the many instruments, and the present verse grounds them in the word of the LORD by Nathan and Gad. Yet even were it granted that instruments were divinely prescribed under the law, Clarke will not allow the inference to Christian worship: the whole spirit and genius of the Christian religion, he contends, are against them, for they have too often been introduced as a substitute for the life and power of religion, and where they most prevail there is least of the power of Christianity — "away with such portentous baubles," he cries, "from the worship of that infinite Spirit who requires his followers to worship him in spirit and in truth."

The witnesses do not, over the history, divide: Gill, Ellicott, and Clarke agree that the music was David's, revived by Hezekiah, and sanctioned by the prophets as the commandment of the LORD. But Clarke stands apart in the use he makes of it, pressing the Old Testament instruments into an argument against their place in the church — a polemic the other witnesses do not raise. Between them they show a king reviving not merely the sacrifices but the song, and grounding that song, as Ellicott insists, in a command that was prophetic and therefore divine; while Clarke, honouring the same history, reads it as a warning that outward music must never be suffered to crowd out the inward worship of the Spirit which alone God seeks.
26:
The Levites take their stand with David's instruments and the priests with their trumpets, and the witnesses note the two distinct companies and how their music was ordered. The reformed John Gill observes that the Levites stood with the instruments of David, invented, directed, and ordered to be used by him, the same named in the verse before. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms that these are the instruments David introduced into the public worship, as at 1 Chronicles 23:5, and remarks that the chronicler's evident interest in the musical portion of the temple ritual receives here one more illustration.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the arrangement of the two bodies. The Levites stood with David's stringed instruments and the priests with the trumpets; and when the sacrifice began, the song of the LORD commenced — the praising of Jahve by song and by the music of the strings — together with the blowing of the trumpets, "under the leading of the instruments of David." This last phrase Keil takes to mean that the trumpet-blast of the priests regulated itself by the playing of the stringed instruments, suiting itself to the song and the music of the Levites, so that the harps and psalteries set the measure and the trumpets fell in with them.

The witnesses do not divide, and the division of labour they describe is worth marking. Two orders of ministers, two kinds of instrument: the Levites with the strings that David had appointed, the priests with the trumpets that the law of Moses had given to the sons of Aaron, each keeping his proper office even in the making of the music, as they had kept it in the cleansing of the house. The trumpets, moreover, were the priests' own by the ancient ordinance of Moses, while the stringed instruments were the Levites' by the later appointment of David, so that in this one concerted music the two great authorities of Israel's worship, the law and the king, sounded together in a single praise. Gill and Ellicott fix the Davidic instruments; Keil sets the priests' trumpets under the lead of the Levites' strings. Between them they show a worship restored in every part and rightly ordered in each — not a confused noise but a concerted praise, the trumpets of the priesthood and the harps of the singers joined in a single music that would break out, at the very moment the burnt-offering ascended, into the song of the LORD. The instruments stand ready; the next verse will sound them.
27:
Hezekiah gives the word, and at the instant the burnt-offering begins the song of the LORD bursts out with it — and the witnesses mark the deliberate joining of sacrifice and praise. The reformed John Gill notes that the burnt-offering was wholly devoted to the LORD, an acknowledgment of his sovereignty over the people and of his goodness to them. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott explains why the command to offer it is repeated here from v.21: all that came between was descriptive of the preparations, and now, the victims slain and flayed and the altar sprinkled and the musicians in their places, everything was ready and the sacrifice was ordered to begin. "At the time when the burnt-offering began, the song of Jehovah began, and the clarions," Ellicott renders, "under the lead of the instruments of David" — the harps and lyres dominant throughout, the trumpets subordinate to their music.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the same simultaneity: the words are repeated from the earlier verse to form the connection, so that when the sacrificial act commenced, the praising of Jahve by song, and the blowing of the trumpets, commenced with it, all under the leading of the stringed instruments. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley turns to the meaning of the song, which he takes to be the psalms composed by David and Asaph, and draws the lesson: even sorrow for sin must not put us out of tune for praising God; by faith we must even then rejoice in the LORD our righteousness, and our prayers and praises must attend upon his offering, to be accepted only in the virtue of it.

The witnesses do not divide, and the exact coincidence they all observe — the song beginning at the instant the offering began — carries the theology of the scene. The praise did not precede the sacrifice, nor follow it at a distance, but rose with the smoke of the burnt-offering from the altar, so that atonement and adoration ascended together. Gill fixes the wholly-devoted offering; Ellicott and Keil trace the strings and trumpets breaking out at the sacrifice's start; Wesley reads the psalms and the faith that sings them. Between them they show a worship in which the song is not an ornament added to the sacrifice but is bound to it, accepted with it, and offered through it — the praise of the people mounting to God upon the merit of the victim, as Wesley says, "accepted only in the virtue of it." It is the picture, in Israel's own courts, of every acceptable praise: a song that dares to rise only because a sacrifice is burning beneath it.
28:
While the offering burns, the whole assembly bows in worship and the music sounds on, and the witnesses dwell on the picture of a nation united in adoration. The reformed John Gill notes that all the congregation worshipped, bowing their heads as a token of divine adoration. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch describe the sustained scene: throughout the offering of the burnt-offering, until it was ended, the whole congregation stood worshipping, and the song of the Levites, accompanied by the music of the stringed instruments and the trumpet-blowing of the priests, continued without pause; "the song was singing," Keil renders the Hebrew idiom, standing for "the body of singers sang," as "the trumpets" stand for the trumpeters.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott presses the same idioms of instrument put for player. "The singers" is literally "the song," as we might say "the music was playing"; "the trumpeters sounded" is properly "the clarions were blowing," the participle masculine though the noun be feminine, because the word really stands for the men who blew them — just as modern orchestras speak of "the violins" or "the cellos," meaning the players. And Ellicott finds the passage highly interesting for the light it throws upon the manner in which the worship of the second temple was conducted in the chronicler's own age, the temple ritual being a matter of immemorial tradition, as the like scene at 2 Chronicles 7:5-6 suggests.

The witnesses do not divide, and the tableau they recover is the still centre of the chapter. Congregation, singers, and trumpeters are held together in a single act: the people prostrate in silent adoration, the Levites lifting the psalm, the priests sounding the clarions, and all of it continuing "until the burnt offering was finished." Gill marks the bowed heads; Keil renders the idiom of song and trumpet; Ellicott recovers the players behind the instruments and the window the verse opens on later temple worship. Between them they show the whole nation gathered into one motion of worship, every order doing its part at once — a unity of praise that answers, ordinance by ordinance, the neglect and division of the reign before. Where Ahaz had shut the doors and silenced the song, his son fills the house with a worship in which king and people, priest and Levite, voice and instrument, all bow together before the God they had forsaken and have now found again.
29:
When the offering is finished, the king and all who were with him bow to the ground, and the witnesses note the solemn close of the sacrificial act. The reformed John Gill observes simply that they had made an end of offering both the sin-offering and the burnt-offering. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch mark the posture: at the conclusion of the sacrificial act the king and all who were present knelt and worshipped — a bowing that gathers up the whole solemnity into a final act of homage. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the word, noting that "bowed themselves" is rather "bowed the knee," the verb of kneeling used at Isaiah 45:23 and 1 Kings 19:18, so that the assembly did not merely incline the head but sank upon their knees before the LORD.

The witnesses do not divide, and the brevity of the notice does not empty it of weight. The sacrifice done, the smoke of the burnt-offering spent, the king does not turn away to other business but leads his people down upon their knees. That the chronicler records the kneeling twice over in this passage — the congregation worshipping while the offering burned, and now king and court kneeling when it was finished — is his way of framing the whole act of atonement in adoration: worship before, worship during, worship after. Keil marks the verb as a contracted form for the ending of the sacrificial act, so that the kneeling is set precisely at the point where the offering is done and the fire has finished its work. Gill fixes the completed offering; Keil and Ellicott recover the bending of the knee. Between them they show a monarch who, having commanded the sacrifice, will not exempt himself from the humility it requires. Hezekiah kneels with the rest; the throne bows with the people; and the re-consecration of the temple reaches its fitting climax not in the king's dignity but in his prostration. It is the answer, in a single gesture, to the fathers who had "turned their backs" upon the house of the LORD: where they had faced away in contempt, the son and his court now kneel down in reverence, their faces to the altar and their knees upon the ground. And the kneeling of the king is itself a sermon: the man who had commanded the whole solemnity, whose word had set priests and Levites and singers to their tasks, bows lowest of all when the sacrifice is done, teaching his people by his own posture that the throne of Judah is itself a subject before the throne of heaven.
30:
The king and the princes bid the Levites sing the praises of the LORD in the words of David and of Asaph, and the witnesses attend to the psalms, the joy, and the title given to the ancient singer. The reformed John Gill notes that they were to make use of psalms composed by the one and the other, taking the song, on Jarchi's guess, to be that which begins "O give thanks unto the LORD, call upon his name." The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read the verse not as a fresh command issued only after the sacrifice, but as a comprehensive conclusion of the whole description: the king and princes commanded the Levites to sing praise with the words of David and Asaph, and they sang with gladness and bowed their heads and worshipped. Keil marks that Asaph is here called a "seer," as Jeduthun is at 2 Chronicles 35:15 and Heman at 1 Chronicles 25:5 — the temple musicians reckoned among the prophets.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott weighs the phrase "with the words of David and of Asaph." It is usually taken to mean that the singing consisted in chanting the psalms of David and Asaph; yet the expression, he notes, may be compared with "by the words of the LORD" at v.15 and "by the commandment of David and Gad" at v.25, and so might mean only that the singing was in accordance with the arrangements David and Asaph had made. "With gladness" he renders "unto exultation," that is, rapturously; and the bowing of the heads he places at the song's end.

So a small difference of reading opens between the witnesses — whether the Levites chanted the actual psalms of David and Asaph, as Gill and Keil assume, or sang merely according to the order those men had established, as Ellicott allows — though the difference touches the manner, not the substance, of the praise. What none of them doubts is the joy of it: the singing rose "unto exultation," the rapturous gladness of a people whose worship had been restored. And the title "seer," which the witnesses recover for Asaph, quietly dignifies the whole musical service: the psalms are not mere art but prophecy set to music, the words of men who spoke for God. Between them the witnesses close the great act of praise as it began, in song — the Levites singing the inspired words with exultant gladness, and bowing, when the song was done, in one last act of worship before the LORD whose house was clean again.
31:
The solemn sacrifices ended, Hezekiah opens the festival's closing act with an invitation to the whole assembly to bring their own offerings, and the witnesses weigh both the consecration he proclaims and the free-hearted giving that answered it. The reformed John Gill notes that the king "answered and said," that is, proceeded to speak. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the force of his opening words, "now ye have filled your hand to the LORD," as meaning "you have consecrated yourselves anew to the service of the LORD," the phrase of priestly consecration used at Exodus 32:29; and they take the summons that follows, "come near and bring sacrifices and thank-offerings," as addressed to the congregation, since it is answered by the notice that the congregation brought them.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agrees that "ye have consecrated" is literally "ye have filled your hand for Jehovah," a phrase used of the consecration of priests at Leviticus 7:37, and here applied to the whole assembly, who had consecrated themselves anew by their presence and their part in the previous solemnities. Others, he allows, would confine the words to the priests, the king then turning to the people with "come near." He distinguishes the offerings named — the sacrifices being thank-offerings, and the thanksgivings a peculiar species of them, accompanied by special psalms — and marks the phrase "as many as were of a free heart," literally "every free-hearted one," as at 1 Chronicles 29:6. Burnt-offerings, Ellicott adds, were a token of greater self-denial than thank-offerings, because they were wholly consumed on the altar, whereas the worshippers feasted upon the latter. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the consecration as reconciliation accomplished — now that they had reconciled themselves and the house to God, and he was ready to accept their sacrifices — and notes that the burnt-offerings showed more generosity than the rest, being wholly burnt and offered to God.

A mild question divides the witnesses: whether "ye have filled your hand" is spoken to the priests alone, whose consecration the phrase properly describes, or to the whole congregation, who had joined in the solemnities — Keil, Ellicott, and Wesley inclining to the wider sense, that the whole people were now consecrated and invited to give. But over the substance they are one. The king does not treat the atonement as a transaction complete in itself; he presses it forward into free and grateful giving, calling a consecrated people to bring their own thank-offerings, and marking with honour those whose full hearts moved them to the costlier burnt-offering that keeps nothing back. Between them the witnesses show the reform passing from the official sacrifice commanded by the throne to the voluntary devotion of the people — worship that began in the king's command ending in the people's willing gift.
32:
The people answer the king's invitation with a great multitude of burnt-offerings, and the witnesses count the tally and mark its meaning. The reformed John Gill records the number the congregation brought — seventy bullocks, a hundred rams, and two hundred lambs — all of them for a burnt-offering to the LORD, of which the offerers kept no part to feast upon but which were wholly devoted to God by way of thankfulness. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm the count and call it very large: seventy bullocks, a hundred rams, two hundred lambs, brought spontaneously by the congregation, before passing on to the still greater number of the thank-offerings that the next verse will name.

The witnesses do not divide, and the figures they reckon are worth pausing over. These were not the sacrifices the king had commanded for the expiation of the kingdom, the sanctuary, and Judah — those were the sevenfold sin-offerings and burnt-offerings of the earlier verses; these are the free gift of the people, brought of their own accord once the king had bidden the free-hearted come near at v.31. And Gill's observation gives the number its weight: every one of these victims was a whole burnt-offering, wholly consumed upon the altar, the offerers reserving nothing for themselves. A people who had lately lain under the wrath of God for the idolatry of Ahaz now pressed forward, unbidden save by the king's general summons, to give back to the LORD a multitude of offerings from which they would gain nothing but the joy of having given. The largeness of the tally is thus a measure of the largeness of the heart behind it. Where the sin-offering had answered the guilt of the past, these burnt-offerings answer the gratitude of the present; and the whole devotion of each victim, holding nothing back, is the fitting emblem of a nation that, having been forgiven much, would now withhold nothing from the God who had received it again. The witnesses let the number stand as it is, and it speaks for itself: It is one thing for a king to command a sacrifice and another for a people to bring one unbidden; and the chronicler, by setting the people's spontaneous seventy and hundred and two hundred beside the sevenfold offering the throne had required, quietly measures how far the reform had already sunk into the nation's heart. The reform that began in the king's resolve had kindled in the people a generosity that overflowed the bare requirement, and offered to God far more than duty asked.
33:
Beyond the burnt-offerings came a still greater number of consecrated victims, and the witnesses distinguish these thank-offerings and weigh the modest scale of the whole.
