The reformed John Gill explains that the consecrated things were those devoted for peace-offerings, of which the owners had a part — six hundred oxen and three thousand sheep. Yet he notes soberly that this was a much smaller number than had been offered on great occasions in the days of David and Solomon, the nation being now poorer; and besides, these were the oblation of only two tribes, and not of all Israel. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch identify the same "consecrated" as the beasts brought for thank-offering, comparing the like usage at 2 Chronicles 35:13 and Nehemiah 10:34, and reckon them at six hundred bullocks and three thousand of the smaller cattle, sheep and goats together.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms briefly that the consecrated things were the victims for the thank-offerings, again citing 2 Chronicles 35:13. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the phrase in the same sense, taking the consecrated things to be all the offerings devoted to God besides the burnt-offerings already mentioned.

The witnesses do not divide, and Gill's two observations give the verse its depth. The peace-offerings differed from the burnt-offerings in that the worshippers shared in them, feasting before the LORD upon what they had brought, so that these three thousand and six hundred victims furnished a great sacred meal for a reconciled people. And yet, Gill reminds us, the number, large as it seems, fell well short of the lavish sacrifices of Judah's wealthier past, for Ahaz had left the kingdom impoverished, and only two tribes now brought their gifts where once all Israel had come. There is, in that quiet comparison, both a sorrow and a hope: a sorrow that the nation was too reduced to match the abundance of David's and Solomon's days, and a hope in the very greatness of what a poor and diminished people yet offered. Keil and Ellicott fix the thank-offerings and their tally; Wesley gathers them with the rest of the consecrated gifts. Between them they show a worship restored not to its former splendour but to its former truth — fewer victims than of old, yet offered by hearts newly reconciled, and shared in a common feast that sealed the peace the day's atonement had made. The comparison Gill draws is not a complaint but a comfort, for it shows that God measures an offering by the heart that brings it and not by the wealth behind it, receiving the diminished gift of a poor and faithful remnant as gladly as the lavish herds of a richer age.
34:
The offerings proved too many for the priests to handle, and the Levites stepped in to help — a circumstance the witnesses read as both a practical shift and a quiet reproach to the priesthood. The reformed John Gill notes that the priests were too few to flay all the burnt-offerings, the taking off of the skins being properly the priests' work. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch explain the law behind the difficulty: in the case of a private burnt-offering the flaying was the offerer's own business, as at Leviticus 1:6, but in sacrifices offered in the name of the congregation it fell to the priests, and in it, since the task was not specifically priestly, the Levites might assist — which they did, until the work was ended and until the other priests had sanctified themselves.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott confirms the point and reads the closing clause pointedly: the Levites helped until the priests as a body had begun to sanctify themselves, "for the Levites were more upright in heart to sanctify themselves than the priests" — the priests, as a class, having probably been more deeply involved in the corruption of the last reign. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads "too few" the same way: not that the priests were few in number, for otherwise they were more than sufficient, but that too few were sanctified and fit for the work; and the Levites' help was a deviation from the strict rule that necessity excused. But it is the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke who dwells longest on the sting of the verse. The priests seem to have been backward in this good work, he observes, while the Levites were more ready to help it forward; why the former should have been so slow is not easy to tell, but it appears to have been the fact. And Clarke draws from it a broad reflection: it often happens that the higher orders of the priesthood are less concerned for the prosperity of true religion than the lower, being too busy with worldly things or too satisfied with secular emoluments — for a rich priesthood, he warns, is not favourable to the depth or the spread of religion, earthly gratifications being often put in the place of divine influences.

The witnesses do not divide over the fact, and Clarke's reflection only sharpens what Ellicott and Wesley also see: that at the very hour of reformation the ordained priests lagged behind the Levites in zeal, being the more compromised by the idolatry they had lately served under Ahaz. Gill and Keil fix the law and the necessity; Ellicott and Wesley trace the priests' unfitness to the corruption of the past reign; Clarke turns it into a warning against a comfortable and worldly clergy. Between them they show a striking reversal — the lesser order more upright than the greater, the Levites more forward to sanctify themselves than the priests — and let it stand as a sober reminder that nearness of office is no guarantee of readiness of heart.
35:
The account of the sacrifices closes with a note of their sheer abundance and its accompaniments, and the witnesses gather the details that explain why so many hands were needed. The reformed John Gill observes that besides the multitude of burnt-offerings, whose skins had to be taken off, there were the meat-offerings and drink-offerings that belonged to each, and the fat of the peace-offerings to be burnt — all of which together made a great deal of business and required many hands. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the verse as giving a further reason why the Levites had to help the priests: the priests were so occupied with the actual service of the altar; and he identifies the accompaniments precisely — the fat of the peace-offerings, which had to be burned upon the burnt-offerings, as prescribed at Leviticus 3:5, and the drink-offerings that belonged to them, as ordered at Numbers 15:1-16.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set the same abundance within the summary that follows it, that with all this — the burnt-offerings in abundance, the fat of the peace-offerings, and the drink-offerings for every burnt-offering — "the service of the house of the LORD was set in order." That closing sentence, which the witnesses let stand as the seal of the whole, is the true point to which the verse tends.

The witnesses do not divide, and their several notes converge on that one great result. The heaping-up of offerings, with all their appointed accompaniments of grain and wine and burning fat, was not confusion but fullness — the visible measure of a worship come flooding back after long drought. Gill counts the labour of it; Ellicott fixes the fat and the drink-offerings and the law that governed each; Keil marks the summary that crowns it. Between them they show the temple service, so lately shut up and defiled, now restored to its whole ordered round: the altar heaped with sacrifice, the fat consumed, the libations poured, every rite in its place and every offering with its due accompaniment. "So the service of the house of the LORD was set in order" — the phrase gathers the entire chapter into itself, for it declares that the great work Hezekiah began by opening the doors is now complete. The house is cleansed, the altar is served, the song is sung, the offerings overflow; and the worship of the God of Israel stands established again in Jerusalem as though the reign of Ahaz had never darkened it.
36:
The chapter ends in joy, and the witnesses read that gladness as a testimony to the hand of God in the swiftness of the whole reform. The reformed John Gill notes that Hezekiah rejoiced, and all the people with him, to see things go on so well, which boded good to them. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the ground of the joy: they rejoiced "over that which God had prepared for the people" — by the purification of the temple and the restoration of the worship of Jahve — and the joy was heightened, Keil observes, by the fact that the thing had been done so suddenly, in a shorter time than any could have looked for.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott weighs the same clause and finds it capable of two senses. It may mean, as Keil takes it, that they rejoiced over that which God had set in order for the people — the long-suspended ordinances of the temple worship; or "for the people" may be the plain object of the verb, so that the sense is "rejoiced because God had prepared the people," turning their hearts. And the suddenness Ellicott renders sharply from the Hebrew: "on a sudden happened the matter," a word found only here; the hand of God was seen in the very speed of the revolution, and in the sudden turn of princes and people alike from indifference to glad alacrity, as at 2 Chronicles 30:12.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses press that this was the work of God upon the heart. Adam Clarke marks that Hezekiah and the people rejoiced because God had prepared their hearts to bring about so great a reformation in so short a time; the king's example and influence were, under God, the grand spring of the whole movement — and Clarke reflects on the power lodged with kings, who are no indifferent beings but must be either a great curse or a great blessing to the people they govern. John Wesley reads the change as nothing less than the finger of the Spirit: it was so great and so sudden a change that the people who but the other day were ready to comply with wicked Ahaz in his idolatry were now free and forward in God's service, whereby it plainly appeared to be the work of God, changing their hearts by his Holy Spirit.

A slight difference of reading runs beneath the agreement — whether God had prepared the ordinances and the occasion "for the people," as Keil and Ellicott's first sense would have it, or had prepared the people themselves, turning their hearts, as Wesley and Clarke and Ellicott's second sense would have it. But over the substance the witnesses are wholly one: the reformation was too great and too swift to be the work of man alone. Gill and Keil fix the joy and its ground; Ellicott recovers the two senses and the note of suddenness; Clarke and Wesley trace the whole to God's preparing of the heart. Between them they close the chapter where it began, in the confession that the LORD alone can prepare the heart of man for vital godliness. Hezekiah opened the doors and gathered the Levites and commanded the sacrifice; but the sudden change of a whole people from the idolatry of Ahaz to the glad service of God was the doing of the Spirit, and the joy that crowns the chapter is the joy of a nation that has felt its own heart turned.
